subject: physiology
title: Endogenous Opioids, Descending Pain Control, and Thermoreception

steps.tx: The central nervous system possesses powerful intrinsic analgesic networks capable of suppressing pain transmission at the spinal level. These mechanisms rely upon naturally synthesized peptide ligands known as **endogenous opioids**, which derive from three major genetically distinct polypeptide precursor molecules: pro-opiomelanocortin, proenkephalin, and prodynorphin.
steps.say: Endogenous opioids are naturally synthesized peptides derived from three distinct genetic precursors.

vis.caption: Opioid receptor distribution across central analgesic and reward neurocircuitry.
vis.alt: Endogenous opioid peptide processing and receptor binding distribution

steps.tx: Endogenous opioid peptides mediate their analgesic actions through specific seven-transmembrane G-protein-coupled receptors classified as mu, delta, and kappa. Binding of beta-endorphin or enkephalin to the **mu-opioid receptor** inhibits adenylyl cyclase, closes presynaptic voltage-gated calcium channels, and opens postsynaptic inwardly rectifying potassium channels, hyperpolarizing pain-relaying neurons.
steps.say: Mu-opioid receptors inhibit calcium influx presynaptically and open potassium channels postsynaptically.

left.title: Presynaptic Opioid Actions
points: Coupled to Gi/o heterotrimeric guanine nucleotide binding proteins
Inhibits presynaptic N-type voltage-gated calcium channels
Blocks calcium-dependent exocytosis of glutamate and substance P
Prevents nociceptive neurotransmitter release into synaptic cleft

right.title: Postsynaptic Opioid Actions
points: Activates G-protein-coupled inwardly rectifying potassium channels (GIRK)
Promotes rapid outward potassium flux along electrochemical gradient
Hyperpolarizes second-order spinothalamic projection neurons
Elevates threshold required to fire ascending nociceptive action potentials

steps.tx: Electrical stimulation of specific brainstem structures produces profound analgesia without impairing tactile or proprioceptive sensation. This descending analgesic system originates within the midbrain **periaqueductal grey matter**, which surrounds the cerebral aqueduct of Sylvius and receives rich inputs from the frontal cortex, amygdala, and ascending spinomesencephalic pain tracts.
steps.say: The midbrain periaqueductal grey triggers descending pathways that strongly inhibit spinal pain transmission.

nodes.label: Cortical, Hypothalamic, and Amygdaloid Projections Excite Periaqueductal Grey (PAG)
PAG Enkephalinergic Neurons Inhibit GABAergic Interneurons, Disinhibiting Output
Excitatory Projections Travel to Rostral Ventromedial Medulla (Nucleus Raphe Magnus)
Serotonergic Fibers Descend Dorsolateral Funiculus to Spinal Dorsal Horn

steps.tx: Axons descending from the periaqueductal grey synapse within the rostral ventromedial medulla, specifically targeting the **nucleus raphe magnus**. Neurons of the raphe magnus send serotonergic projections down the spinal dorsolateral funiculus to terminate in the superficial dorsal horn, where they excite enkephalin-releasing interneurons to suppress incoming nociceptive signals.
steps.say: Nucleus raphe magnus sends descending serotonergic fibers to activate spinal enkephalinergic interneurons.

nodes.label: Serotonergic and Noradrenergic Axons Descend Dorsolateral Spinal Cord
Axons Synapse in Rexed Laminae II and III (Substantia Gelatinosa)
Local Enkephalinergic Interneurons Release Met-Enkephalin and Leu-Enkephalin
Inhibits Presynaptic C Fibers and Postsynaptic Spinothalamic Projection Neurons

steps.tx: In parallel with the midline serotonergic descending pathway, noradrenergic neurons located in the dorsolateral pontine tegmentum contribute powerfully to spinal antinociception. Cells within the **locus coeruleus** project descending axons to the dorsal horn, where norepinephrine release binds alpha-two adrenergic receptors to hyperpolarize projection neurons and blunt pain transmission.
steps.say: Locus coeruleus noradrenergic fibers bind alpha-two receptors in the dorsal horn to suppress pain.

vis.caption: Widespread central pain processing demonstrating deficits in descending inhibitory noradrenergic circuits.
vis.alt: Central pain sensitization and failure of descending noradrenergic inhibition

steps.tx: Following focal cutaneous tissue trauma, the uninjured surrounding skin exhibits heightened sensitivity to subsequent mechanical stimuli. Termed **primary versus secondary hyperalgesia**, primary hyperalgesia occurs directly within the injured tissue due to peripheral receptor sensitization, whereas secondary hyperalgesia arises in adjacent uninjured tissue through dorsal horn central sensitization.
steps.say: Primary hyperalgesia is peripheral sensitization at the wound, while secondary hyperalgesia is central spinal sensitization.

left.title: Primary Hyperalgesia
points: Confined strictly to the site of tissue injury and burn
Driven by local inflammatory soup (bradykinin, PGE2, histamine)
Decreased activation threshold of peripheral nociceptors
Responds to both thermal and mechanical stimuli

right.title: Secondary Hyperalgesia
points: Extends into normal undamaged tissue surrounding the injury
Driven by spinal dorsal horn neuroplasticity (central sensitization)
Low-threshold A-beta mechanoreceptors evoke perceived pain (allodynia)
Characteristically responds to mechanical, not thermal, stimuli

steps.tx: Cutaneous temperature is monitored across the body surface by specialized bare nerve endings that respond differentially to warm and cool environmental shifts. These **thermoreceptors** exhibit continuous tonic firing at static skin temperatures, increasing their discharge rate rapidly when skin temperature changes before adapting partially to maintain a steady firing plateau.
steps.say: Cutaneous thermoreceptors monitor temperature through distinct cold and warm receptors with steady resting discharges.

nodes.label: Skin Temperature Fluctuates Within Normal Physiological Range (15-45 C)
Temperature-Sensitive TRP Ion Channels Gated by Thermal Energy Changes
Sudden Temperature Shift Evokes Intense Dynamic Phase Frequency Burst
Receptors Adapt to Slower Static Firing Plateau Signaling Maintained Temperature

steps.tx: Cold and warmth detection relies upon distinct sensory afferent populations expressing different transient receptor potential ion channels. Cold receptors, mediated by thin A-delta and C fibers expressing TRPM8, fire maximally around twenty-five degrees Celsius, whereas warm receptors, mediated exclusively by unmyelinated C fibers expressing TRPV3 and TRPV4, fire between **thirty and forty-three degrees Celsius**.
steps.say: Cold receptors peak at twenty-five degrees, while warm receptors fire between thirty and forty-three degrees Celsius.

left.title: Cold Thermoreceptors
points: Outnumber warm receptors by 4 to 10-fold across human skin
Conducted via thinly myelinated A-delta and unmyelinated C fibers
Mediated by menthol-sensitive TRPM8 and TRPA1 channels
Operate between 10 and 38 C, peaking around 25 to 30 C

right.title: Warm Thermoreceptors
points: Less numerous, distributed more sparsely across cutaneous surface
Conducted exclusively over unmyelinated C nerve fibers
Mediated by heat-sensitive TRPV3 and TRPV4 cation channels
Operate between 30 and 45 C, peaking around 42 to 43 C
